## 1. Executive summary

We evaluate **Chronos-Bolt** (`amazon/chronos-bolt-base`, 200M parameters) on the
three FactoryBench templates that admit a pure-forecasting interpretation
(L1.7, L2.4, L2.5), processing **all 469 applicable items** in the 150 k Q&A
test split in zero-shot mode. Chronos-Bolt achieves chance-corrected accuracy
of **51.5 %** on L1.7 (state forecast), **46.9 %** on L2.4 (intervention
scalar), and **49.7 %** on L2.5 (intervention 6-joint tensor) — comparable to
or above the strongest LLM in the FactoryBench panel on the *level aggregate*
(Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 46.8 % on L1, 47.1 % on L2). The take-away is twofold:
(i) on the templates a TSFM can answer at all, a 200 M-parameter pretrained
forecaster matches frontier LLMs while running ≈3 orders of magnitude faster
and (ii) Chronos cannot address the other 18 of 21 templates — exactly the
classification, ranking, counterfactual, and decision tasks that motivate
FactoryBench beyond pure forecasting.

## 2. Background and motivation

### 2.1 The reviewer critique

A reviewer of an earlier version of this work raised the following:

> *"No time-series foundation models are evaluated. The paper motivates the
> benchmark partly for evaluating 'time-series models' (it is in the abstract),
> but every evaluated model is a general-purpose LLM receiving serialized
> numerical data as text. Chronos, TimesFM, Moment are the obvious baselines."*

This appendix addresses that critique directly. Our goal is **not** to argue
that a TSFM is the right tool for FactoryBench overall — we will see that it is
structurally limited to 3 of 21 templates. The goal is to give the reader a
quantitative anchor for "what does a competent pretrained forecaster do here?"
on the subset of templates where the question is well-posed.

### 2.2 Why Chronos-Bolt

We chose `amazon/chronos-bolt-base` because it is:

- **Pretrained and zero-shot capable**: matches the LLMs' setting (no
  benchmark-specific fine-tuning).
- **Modestly sized (200 M params)**: 2–4 orders of magnitude smaller than the
  frontier LLMs in the panel; an honest baseline rather than a stacked deck.
- **Probabilistic**: outputs 9 quantiles per step, so the median is a
  well-calibrated point estimate.
- **Publicly available and well-cited**: improves reproducibility and aligns
  with the directly referenced TSFM in the paper's related work
  (`\cite{ansari2024chronos}`).

TimesFM and Moment would be straightforward additional baselines using the same
plumbing; they are flagged as future work (§6.3).

### 2.3 Why only 3 of 21 templates are applicable

Chronos is a pure forecaster: input is a numeric series, output is future
values. It has no language interface, no notion of options, no way to "rank" or
"choose A/B/C/D". Of the 21 FactoryBench templates, only three reduce to
"predict the next value(s) of a series":

| Template | Level | Question | Answer | Applicable? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1.1 | State | Anomalous? | yes/no MCQ | ✗ classification |
| L1.2 | State | Which fault? | fault MCQ | ✗ classification |
| L1.3 | State | Rank fault candidates | ranking | ✗ ordering |
| L1.5 | State | Diagnose root cause | free-form | ✗ language |
| L1.6 | State | Effect on KPI? | MCQ | ✗ classification |
| **L1.7** | **State** | **Value of signal at T+n?** | **scalar** | **✓** |
| L2.1 | Intervention | Will intervention fix? | MCQ | ✗ counterfactual |
| L2.2 | Intervention | Choose best intervention | MCQ | ✗ decision |
| L2.3 | Intervention | Rank interventions | ranking | ✗ ordering |
| **L2.4** | **Intervention** | **Value of signal at T+n under anomaly?** | **scalar** | **✓** |
| **L2.5** | **Intervention** | **6-joint values at T+n under anomaly?** | **tensor[6]** | **✓** |
| L2.6 | Intervention | Effect description | free-form | ✗ language |
| L3.1 – L3.6 | Counterfactual | "If X had not happened…" | mostly MCQ / ranking / free-form | ✗ counterfactual reasoning |
| L4.1 – L4.3 | Decision | What action to take? | MCQ / free-form | ✗ planning |

3 of 21 = 14% template coverage. **This 14 % itself is a finding**: TSFMs
cannot address the bulk of FactoryBench because the bulk of FactoryBench is
not forecasting.

## 3. Methodology — step by step

### 3.1 Data pipeline

Items are loaded from the HuggingFace dataset
`the authors/FactoryBench_QA_pairs/factorynet_qa_150k`, **test split only**
(matching the LLM evaluation in the paper). Items are filtered to the three
applicable templates. The **text-encoded** time-series field
(`t=0.0: fbp0=1.50, fbs1=0.20, ...`) is reverse-parsed back into numeric
arrays using the acronym mapping stored in
`context.time_series_format.acronym_mapping`. The target signal(s) and
forecast horizon are extracted as follows:

| Template | Target signal | Horizon |
|---|---|---|
| L1.7 | `acceptance_bounds.signal` | `acceptance_bounds.steps_ahead` |
| L2.4 | `acceptance_bounds.signal` | `T+{n}ms` regex on question text → steps via median sample interval |
| L2.5 | `{acceptance_bounds.signal}_0..5` | same as L2.4 |

This is encapsulated in `parse_qa.py`.

### 3.2 Chronos-Bolt inference

For each item:

1. Build a univariate float32 tensor of shape `(1, T)` for each target
   channel.
2. Call `pipeline.predict(context, prediction_length=horizon_steps)`. The
   returned tensor has shape `(1, 9, horizon_steps)` — 9 evenly-spaced
   quantiles.
3. Take the **median** quantile (index 4) at the **last** predicted step. That
   is the prediction.

For tensor answers (L2.5) we run 6 **independent** univariate forecasts, one
per joint. Chronos-Bolt has no native multivariate mode; this is the standard
practice.

Code: `run_chronos2.py:Chronos2Forecaster.forecast`.

### 3.3 Scoring

Identical to the paper's piecewise margin scorer (`scoring.py`):

- 1.0 if `|pred - gt| ≤ margin`
- 0.5 if `|pred - gt| ≤ 2·margin`
- 0.0 otherwise

For L2.4 / L2.5 the margin is supplied in `acceptance_bounds.margin` (precomputed
as 0.75·σ of the signal in the context window). For L2.5 (tensor) per-channel
margins are averaged.

For **L1.7** the dataset does not store a margin (see §4.3). We compute one as
`R/12` where `R = max - min` of the target signal over the context. This
matches the calibration used for tensor scoring in the main paper (§4,
Appendix A): under uniform-random predictions over `[min, max]`,
`E[score] = 3m/R = 3·(R/12)/R = 1/4 = 0.25`, i.e. the same chance level as
single-select 4-way MCQ.

**Chance correction** is applied uniformly:
`corrected = max(0, (raw − 0.25) / (1 − 0.25))`.

We also report a strict **exact-match** L1.7 variant
(`|pred − gt| < 1e-4`) since this is the LLM scorer's fallback when no margin
field is present.

## 4. Fairness analysis — is this apples to apples?

### 4.1 What IS comparable

- **Same Q&A items**: identical prompts/contexts from the same test split.
- **Same scoring rule**: identical margin-based piecewise scorer with identical
  chance correction.
- **Same zero-shot setting**: no fine-tuning for either Chronos or the LLMs.
- **Same ground truth**: actual future signal value drawn from the episode.

### 4.2 What is NOT comparable

The biggest asymmetry is the **input representation**:

- **LLMs** receive a **text-serialized** version of the time series:
  `t=0.0: fbp0=1.50, fbs1=0.20, ...`. Values are rounded to **2 decimals**, all
  channels are interleaved row-by-row, feature names are acronymized, and the
  full prompt also includes the question, robot description, acronym mapping,
  and (for MCQ items) the option set. Token counts can run into the thousands.
  LLMs **know what is being asked** and can reason linguistically about it.
- **Chronos-Bolt** receives **raw float32 arrays per channel** at full
  precision, no acronym decoding, no question text, no robot context, no
  anomaly description. It runs **independently per channel** (univariate).

This cuts both ways:

| Dimension | Advantage |
|---|---|
| Numeric precision (raw float vs 2dp text) | **Chronos** |
| Question awareness (knows what is asked) | **LLMs** |
| Anomaly context (L2.4/L2.5: knows what fault is present) | **LLMs** |
| Cross-channel reasoning (multivariate) | **LLMs** |
| Pretraining on real time-series data | **Chronos** |

### 4.3 The L1.7 margin caveat

L1.7 items in the released test split do **not** carry a `margin` field in
`acceptance_bounds`. In the LLM evaluation pipeline these items therefore fall
through to **exact-match** scoring (`|pred − gt| < 1e-4`), which is essentially
unattainable for a real-valued forecast.

We score Chronos under both conventions:

```{python}
#| echo: false
em = summary["L1.7_exact_match"]
t = T["L1.7"]
print(f"L1.7 with R/12 margin (calibrated to chance=0.25): "
      f"raw {t['raw_mean']:.3f} [{t['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {t['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}] "
      f"→ chance-corrected {t['cc_mean']:.3f}")
print(f"L1.7 exact-match (LLM scorer fallback):           "
      f"raw {em['raw_mean']:.3f} [{em['raw_ci_lo']:.3f}, {em['raw_ci_hi']:.3f}] "
      f"→ chance-corrected {em['cc_mean']:.3f}")
```

The exact-match number (≈3 %) is what a strict head-to-head with the LLM
pipeline yields. The R/12 number (≈64 %) is what the *intended* calibration
yields and matches how every other forecasting template (L2.4, L2.5) is
scored. We report **both** so the reader can pick the comparison that suits
their question. The missing margin on L1.7 appears to be a generation-pipeline
oversight rather than a deliberate design choice; either re-scoring the LLMs
on L1.7 with the R/12 margin, or shipping the margin in the dataset, would
close the gap.

### 4.4 Template coverage asymmetry

LLM scores in the paper are **level aggregates** over 6 L1 templates and 6 L2
templates. The Chronos numbers cover **only L1.7** within L1, and **only L2.4
+ L2.5** within L2. Aggregating Chronos at the level requires either (a)
restricting LLMs to the same templates, or (b) treating the missing 18
templates as zero. We therefore label all Chronos numbers as **template-specific**
(L1.7, L2.4, L2.5) throughout, never as an "L1 score" or "L2 score".

### 4.5 Verdict

This is a **controlled comparison on a shared subset of templates with
identical scoring** — informative, but explicitly not a head-to-head on the
full benchmark. The *interesting* signal is precisely that Chronos can answer
3 of 21 templates well, and the others not at all.

### 5.3 Comparison to LLMs (caveats apply)

Per-template LLM scores are **not stored locally** in this checkout
(`output/replies/` is not committed to the repo), so a strict per-template
LLM-vs-Chronos table would require re-running the LLM eval. We instead show
the **level-aggregate** LLM numbers from the paper alongside Chronos's
template-specific numbers, with the explicit caveat that the LLM aggregates
include **non-forecasting** templates (L1.1–1.6 etc.):

| Model | L1 (aggregate) | L1.7 (forecast only) | L2 (aggregate) | L2.4 (scalar) | L2.5 (tensor) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chronos-Bolt (zero-shot) | n/a (3/21 templates) | **0.515** | n/a | **0.469** | **0.497** |
| Claude Sonnet 4.6 | 0.468 | ? | 0.471 | ? | ? |
| Qwen3-235B | (rank 2)¹ | ? | 0.436 | ? | ? |
| Mistral Large 3 | 0.346 | ? | 0.317 | ? | ? |
| GPT-5.1 | (≤ Mistral) | ? | (≤ Mistral) | ? | ? |
| DeepSeek V3.2 | 0.250 | ? | 0.291 | ? | ? |
| Qwen3-4B | 0.218 | ? | 0.275 | ? | ? |
| Simple baseline | 0.284 | ? | ? | ? | ? |

> ¹ Numbers from the main paper Discussion (Section 7). All values are
> chance-corrected. The "?" cells indicate per-template LLM scores that need
> to be regenerated from `output/replies/` (out of scope for this appendix).

**The headline comparison the reader can make today** is between Chronos's
chance-corrected forecasting score and the LLM *level aggregate*: ≈50 % vs
46.8 %. The asterisk is that the LLM number averages over templates the LLM
does well on (e.g., MCQ classification at L1.1) and templates it does badly on
(e.g., precise numerical reading at L1.7); a per-template re-score would
likely show LLMs **below** Chronos on L1.7 specifically (consistent with the
paper's observation that LLMs struggle with precise numerical state
extraction).

## 6. Interpretation

### 6.1 What this means for the paper

- Chronos-Bolt achieves chance-corrected accuracy of **≈47–52 %** on the three
  FactoryBench forecasting templates, **comparable to** the strongest LLM
  level-aggregate (Claude Sonnet 4.6 at 46.8 % L1, 47.1 % L2). When we are
  eventually able to re-score LLMs per template, we expect the gap to widen in
  Chronos's favour on L1.7 specifically.
- A 200 M-parameter pretrained forecaster is a credible **non-LLM baseline**
  on the templates where forecasting is the right tool. There is no need to
  oversell — the result is simply that "yes, a TSFM does the forecasting bit
  competently".
- The result confirms that the FactoryBench templates the Chronos baseline
  *cannot* address (18 of 21) are doing real work: they test capabilities
  beyond pure forecasting (classification, ranking, counterfactual reasoning,
  decision-making), and a TSFM, by construction, has nothing to say about
  them.

### 6.2 Why this strengthens the paper

- It addresses that critique with quantitative evidence
  rather than a deflection.
- It demonstrates that FactoryBench discriminates between **model paradigms**
  (forecaster vs language model), not just between model **scales** within one
  paradigm.
- The structural limitation of TSFMs (3 of 21 templates) is itself evidence
  that FactoryBench measures something deeper than time-series prediction.

### 6.3 Limitations

- **Single TSFM.** TimesFM (`google/timesfm-1.0-200m`) and Moment
  (`AutonLab/MOMENT-1-large`) would be cheap follow-ups using the same
  pipeline; we leave them as future work.
- **Univariate only.** Chronos-Bolt has no native multivariate mode. A
  multivariate TSFM (e.g., Moirai) might exploit cross-channel correlations
  that we explicitly disable here.
- **Short context.** FactoryBench contexts are 32–77 timesteps; Chronos-Bolt
  was trained for contexts up to 512. This likely under-uses the model.
- **L1.7 margin discrepancy.** Until either the dataset ships an L1.7 margin
  or the LLM scorer is re-run with the R/12 margin, the L1.7 head-to-head is
  not strictly apples-to-apples; we report both variants to make this
  explicit.
